prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: The octopus relies on its keen color vision to match the exact colors of its surroundings.
choices.rationale: The passage says the octopus is colorblind, not keen-sighted.

choices.text: The octopus changes color mainly to communicate with other nearby octopuses.
choices.rationale: Communication between octopuses is never mentioned.

choices.text: The octopus shifts color slowly, building up a disguise over many minutes.
choices.rationale: The change happens in under a second, not over many minutes.

choices.text: The octopus changes color through a muscular pigment system it cannot itself see.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage centers on the surprising mechanism of color change in a colorblind animal.

explanation: The passage builds toward the paradox of an animal that produces colors it cannot perceive.

stimulus.title: The Color of Thought
stimulus.text: An octopus has no bones and, oddly, almost no color of its own. Yet in less than a second it can flush deep red with alarm or fade to match the speckled gray of a stone. Beneath its skin lie millions of tiny sacs of pigment, each ringed by muscle. When the muscles pull, the sacs widen and color blooms; when they relax, the color vanishes. Stranger still, the octopus is colorblind, so it cannot see the very hues it produces. Some researchers suspect its skin itself senses light, letting the animal paint a disguise it can never admire.

prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Accurate maps were achieved gradually, replacing guesses with hard-won measurements.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage traces the replacement of guesses by measurements and honors the effort behind it.

choices.text: Mapmakers of the past genuinely believed that sea monsters filled the unexplored oceans.
choices.rationale: The passage says monsters were decoration 'less from belief.'

choices.text: Explorers of the period actually preferred to use inaccurate, guesswork maps.
choices.rationale: Explorers corrected maps; they did not prefer errors.

choices.text: Maps drawn in earlier centuries in fact contained no errors of any kind.
choices.rationale: The passage describes early errors.

explanation: The passage's point is the slow, effortful move from guesswork to accuracy.

stimulus.title: The Edge of the Map
stimulus.text: Old maps are full of guesses. Where knowledge ran out, mapmakers filled the blank spaces with mountains they had never seen and coastlines that bent the wrong way. Some added sea monsters, less from belief than from a need to decorate the unknown. As explorers returned with measurements, the guesses were slowly corrected, and the monsters swam off the page. But a finished, accurate map can hide how hard it was to make. Every clean line was once a question, settled only by someone willing to sail past the edge of what was known and come back with an answer.

prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: Tomas decides he no longer misses his hometown now that he has moved.
choices.rationale: The passage shows he does miss home, not that he stopped.

choices.text: Tomas writes the letters mainly to impress the friends in his new city.
choices.rationale: The letters are addressed home, not aimed at impressing new friends.

choices.text: Writing an unsent letter helps Tomas privately acknowledge his homesickness.
choices.rationale: Correct. The closing lines show the unsent writing let him admit his homesickness.

choices.text: Tomas mails the most honest of his three letters to his family at last.
choices.rationale: He keeps the letter folded in a drawer rather than mailing it.

explanation: The narrative resolves on writing as a way to admit feelings to himself.

stimulus.title: The Unsent Letter
stimulus.text: Tomas wrote the letter three times before he stopped trying to send it. In the first version he was cheerful, listing the small triumphs of his new city as if homesickness were a thing he had outgrown. In the second he was honest, and the page filled with everything he missed until it embarrassed him. The third version said almost nothing at all. He kept that one folded in a drawer. Months later he found it again and realized the words he could not send had still done their work: writing them had let him admit, if only to himself, how far from home he truly felt.

prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: A frozen seed vault preserves crop diversity as a backup against future losses.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage explains the vault as a rarely used backup that protects crop variety.

choices.text: Seeds kept in the frozen vault lose the ability to sprout within about a year.
choices.rationale: The cold lets seeds sprout even after decades.

choices.text: The mountain vault was built mainly to store bars of gold rather than seeds.
choices.rationale: It values seeds 'more than gold,' figuratively.

choices.text: The frozen seed vault is opened and drawn upon by its keepers nearly every single day.
choices.rationale: The keepers hope it is rarely needed.

explanation: The passage frames the vault as a safeguard for crop diversity.

stimulus.title: A Vault for Seeds
stimulus.text: Deep inside a frozen mountain, a vault holds something more valuable than gold: seeds. Hundreds of thousands of varieties of crops, gathered from around the world, rest in sealed packets at temperatures far below freezing. The cold slows the seeds' aging to a crawl, so that even after decades they can still sprout. The vault is a backup. If a war, flood, or disease wipes out a crop somewhere, a sample can be withdrawn and grown again. Its keepers hope it will rarely be needed, the way one hopes never to use a fire extinguisher. Its value lies precisely in being ready and almost never used.

prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Lighthouse keepers were never really necessary for the lights to function properly.
choices.rationale: Keepers performed essential tasks for centuries.

choices.text: Modern lighthouses still need a keeper to climb the tower every night.
choices.rationale: Automation withdrew the keepers.

choices.text: Automation made lighthouses more reliable but ended the human role of the keeper.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage contrasts improved reliability with the loss of the human keeper.

choices.text: Lighthouses stopped working and went dark once automation was introduced.
choices.rationale: The lights 'still shine,' more reliably than before.

explanation: The passage balances technical gain against a human loss.

stimulus.title: Keeping the Light
stimulus.text: For centuries, a lighthouse meant a keeper. Someone had to climb the tower each night, trim the wick, polish the lens, and wind the clockwork that turned the light. Storms made the work dangerous, and isolation made it lonely, but ships depended on that faithful beam. In the twentieth century, automation arrived. Electric lamps, timers, and remote sensors took over the tasks one by one, and keepers were gradually withdrawn. The lights still shine, more reliably than ever, yet something human slipped away with the last keeper. The machines kept the promise of the light; they could not keep its company.

prompt: Which choice best captures the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: A fine instrument reveals the skill Nadia had built through her earlier struggle.
choices.rationale: Correct. The closing lines tie the fine violin to the skill she had quietly built.

choices.text: Battered school instruments teach a student more than fine instruments ever could.
choices.rationale: The passage shows the loaner as finer than her battered school violin.

choices.text: Nadia's teacher refuses to let her borrow the fine loaner violin at all.
choices.rationale: The teacher hands her the loaner rather than refusing.

choices.text: Nadia decides to give up the violin entirely once the recital has ended.
choices.rationale: She does not quit; she gains insight.

explanation: The narrative resolves on the idea that her growth, not just the violin, produced the beautiful playing.

stimulus.title: The Borrowed Violin
stimulus.text: Nadia had practiced on a school instrument so battered that two of its pegs slipped during every lesson. When her teacher handed her a loaner violin for the recital, she nearly refused; it felt wrong to play something so fine. But as she drew the bow across the strings, the tone opened like a window onto a bright street. Notes she had fought for all year now arrived easily, as if the instrument had been waiting for her. Afterward, returning it to its case, she understood that her old struggles had not been wasted. The fine violin had simply revealed the player she had quietly become.

prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Glass is endlessly recyclable in principle, but flawed systems keep much of it from reuse.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage contrasts glass's ideal recyclability with system failures.

choices.text: Glass, unlike most materials, simply cannot be recycled by any method at all.
choices.rationale: It says glass can be remade again and again.

choices.text: Sorting glass by color is the one step that actually makes recycling glass impossible to do.
choices.rationale: Color sorting is offered as a solution, not an obstacle to recycling.

choices.text: Glass loses a noticeable amount of its quality each time it is recycled again.
choices.rationale: The passage says glass keeps its quality when remade.

explanation: The passage's point is the gap between glass's ideal recyclability and imperfect systems.

stimulus.title: The Endless Material
stimulus.text: Glass has a quiet superpower: it can be melted down and remade again and again without losing quality. A bottle recycled today can become a bottle next month, then another after that, in a loop that, in principle, never wears out. Compared with this ideal, reality lags. Much glass still ends up in landfills because collection is uneven and because mixing colors lowers the value of the recycled material. Sorting by color and keeping glass out of general trash would let more of it re-enter the loop. The material is willing; it is our systems, the author suggests, that need redesigning.

prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Salt marshes release large amounts of stored carbon into the warming air.
choices.rationale: The roots store carbon rather than releasing it.

choices.text: Salt marshes are beautiful landscapes that people have always admired for their scenery.
choices.rationale: The passage calls the marsh drab and once-overlooked, not always admired.

choices.text: Draining marshes is the most effective way to defend homes from storms.
choices.rationale: Draining marshes removed protection rather than providing it.

choices.text: Plain-looking salt marshes provide valuable protection that was long overlooked.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage shows the drab marsh doing protective work long unappreciated.

explanation: The passage reveals the overlooked marsh as a valuable natural protector.

stimulus.title: The Quiet Buffer
stimulus.text: Where the land meets the sea, a salt marsh can look like wasteland: flat, muddy, and crossed by winding channels. Yet this drab landscape does remarkable work. Its dense grasses slow incoming waves, blunting the force of storms before they reach homes inland. The same grasses trap sediment, letting the marsh build itself upward as the sea slowly rises. Beneath the mud, roots store carbon that might otherwise warm the air. For years, marshes were drained and filled without much thought. Only later did people recognize that the unglamorous marsh had been protecting them all along, asking nothing in return.

prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Bats can detect only objects that are holding completely still, never ones that are moving.
choices.rationale: Bats detect motion through shifts in the returning sound.

choices.text: Bats produce sounds that humans can easily hear during the night.
choices.rationale: The calls are often too high for humans to hear.

choices.text: Bats perceive their surroundings in the dark by interpreting echoes of their own calls.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage explains how bats build a sound-based picture from echoes.

choices.text: Bats rely chiefly on their sharp eyesight to hunt insects after dark.
choices.rationale: The passage describes hunting by sound, not eyesight.

explanation: The passage centers on echolocation as a sound-built perception of the world.

stimulus.title: Seeing With Sound
stimulus.text: A bat hunting in pitch darkness does not bump into things. It calls out, often at pitches too high for humans to hear, and listens for the echoes that bounce back. From the delay between call and echo, the bat judges how far away an object is; from subtle shifts in the returning sound, it can tell whether the object is moving toward it or away. A moth's fluttering wing returns a different echo than a still leaf. So precise is this sense that some bats can snatch an insect from the air in total darkness. The world the bat perceives is built entirely of sound, a picture painted with echoes.

prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Honeybees actually speak to one another inside the hive using a range of distinct vocal sounds.
choices.rationale: The passage stresses communication 'without sound.'

choices.text: The honeybee's waggle dance carries no consistent or reliable meaning at all.
choices.rationale: The dance reliably encodes specific information.

choices.text: Honeybees locate rich patches of flowers almost entirely by chance and luck.
choices.rationale: The dance communicates location, not luck.

choices.text: The honeybee's waggle dance is a symbolic code for a food source's direction and distance.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage explains how the dance encodes direction and distance.

explanation: The passage frames the waggle dance as a precise symbolic language.

stimulus.title: Dances in the Dark
stimulus.text: A foraging honeybee that finds a rich patch of flowers cannot simply tell the hive where to go. Instead, it dances. On the vertical comb, in darkness, the bee runs a straight line while waggling its body, then loops back to repeat the move. The angle of that straight run, measured against the pull of gravity, encodes the direction of the flowers relative to the sun. The length of the run signals distance. Watching bees crowd around and follow, researchers realized they were seeing a kind of symbolic language, one that passes precise information without sight, sound, or a single spoken word.

prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Fog almost never holds enough moisture to be worth trying to collect at all.
choices.rationale: The passage says nets can collect many liters.

choices.text: Fog nets can completely replace every other source of water in any location.
choices.rationale: The passage calls it a supplement, not a universal replacement.

choices.text: Fog nets can supply useful drinking water in suitable coastal areas, within real limits.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage presents fog harvesting as useful where conditions fit, while noting limits.

choices.text: Harvesting water from fog demands complex machinery and a steady supply of electrical power.
choices.rationale: It relies on gravity and simple mesh, not complex machinery.

explanation: The balanced claim is that fog nets work well in the right setting but are not a cure-all.

stimulus.title: Catching Water From Air
stimulus.text: In a few dry coastal regions, drinking water can be harvested from fog. Tall mesh nets are strung across hillsides where moist air rolls in from the sea. As the fog drifts through, droplets cling to the mesh, merge, and trickle down into troughs and storage tanks. A single large net can collect many liters on a good day, enough to supplement a village's supply. The method is not a cure-all: it works only where fog is frequent and winds are steady, and the nets need upkeep. Yet in the right place, it turns a passing cloud into a dependable resource, using little more than gravity and patience.

prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Sea otters are harmful pests that destroy the kelp forests they live in.
choices.rationale: Otters protect the kelp; their loss lets urchins destroy it.

choices.text: Kelp forests are found mainly in warm, sandy waters near tropical beaches.
choices.rationale: The passage places these forests off cool, rocky coasts.

choices.text: Giant kelp grows so slowly that it can take many years to reach the surface.
choices.rationale: The passage says kelp grows astonishingly fast, not slowly.

choices.text: Kelp forests are rich but fragile habitats that depend on a balance of species.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage presents kelp forests as rich habitats whose health rests on species balance.

explanation: The passage frames kelp forests as productive yet fragile, balanced ecosystems.

stimulus.title: Forests Beneath the Waves
stimulus.text: Off some cool, rocky coasts grow forests that no hiker will ever walk through. Giant kelp, anchored to the seafloor, can stretch dozens of meters toward the surface, swaying in the current like trees in wind. These kelp forests shelter fish, snails, and otters, much as a woodland shelters birds and deer. The kelp grows astonishingly fast, sometimes half a meter in a single day, drinking sunlight near the surface. But the forest is fragile. Where otters vanish, sea urchins multiply and graze the kelp down to bare rock, leaving a barren the divers call an urchin desert. A single missing animal can unmake a whole forest.

prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: Coral bands preserve a long, readable record of past ocean conditions.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage centers on how coral bands record and reveal past conditions.

choices.text: Coral grows faster than trees and so makes a more accurate calendar.
choices.rationale: The passage compares coral to trees but never claims it grows faster.

choices.text: Researchers prefer studying coral because it is easier than studying trees.
choices.rationale: No claim of relative ease over tree study is made.

choices.text: Warm water is the only factor that determines how thick a coral band grows.
choices.rationale: Chemistry and season both matter; warmth is not called the only factor.

explanation: The passage frames the coral as a centuries-long record that researchers learn to read.

stimulus.title: The Coral That Keeps Time
stimulus.text: A coral skeleton grows in fine bands, much like the rings of a tree. In bright, warm months the coral lays down thick layers; in cooler, dimmer months the layers thin. By slicing a coral and counting these bands, researchers can read a record of past seasons stretching back centuries. Even better, the chemistry trapped in each band hints at the water's temperature when it formed. So a single old coral can serve as a kind of diary, written not in words but in stone, recording conditions long before anyone thought to measure them. The challenge is learning to read a language no one designed to be read.

prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Wind is the only means by which any plant can spread its seeds.
choices.rationale: The passage describes wind, hooks, and fruit, not wind alone.

choices.text: Plants are able to uproot themselves and walk to find better ground.
choices.rationale: The passage opens by noting a plant cannot walk.

choices.text: Seeds always grow best directly beneath the shade of the parent plant.
choices.rationale: The passage says seeds need to leave the parent's shadow.

choices.text: Plants have evolved varied methods to disperse their seeds away from the parent.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage surveys several strategies plants use to move their seeds.

explanation: The passage's focus is the variety of seed-dispersal strategies.

stimulus.title: Travelers Without Legs
stimulus.text: A plant cannot walk, yet its seeds must somehow leave the shadow of the parent and find open ground. Evolution has answered this need with a surprising range of tricks. Some seeds grow papery wings and spin away on the wind like tiny helicopters. Others wear hooks that snag the fur of passing animals, hitching a ride for miles. Still others hide inside sweet fruit, counting on an animal to eat them and carry them off, depositing them far away. Each method is a kind of bargain struck with the world around the plant. The seed that travels farthest is often the one with the best chance to grow where the parent's shade cannot reach.

prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: The secret ballot freed voters to choose without fear of pressure or retaliation.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage explains how private ballots protected voters from pressure.

choices.text: Public voting by show of hands gave ordinary workers the most power.
choices.rationale: Public voting invited pressure on workers, reducing their power.

choices.text: Reformers opposed the printed ballot as an unnecessary change.
choices.rationale: Reformers pushed for the printed ballot, not against it.

choices.text: Voting has always been conducted privately, in every place and period of recorded history.
choices.rationale: The passage says voting was long public, not always private.

explanation: The passage's point is that the secret ballot protected the ordinary voter's free choice.

stimulus.title: The Secret Ballot
stimulus.text: It is easy to assume voting has always been private, but for a long time it was not. In many places people voted aloud or by a show of hands, in full view of employers, landlords, and neighbors. That openness invited pressure: a worker might think twice before voting against a boss who could see the choice. Reformers pushed for a printed ballot, marked alone and dropped in a box, so that no one need fear retaliation for an honest vote. The change seemed minor, a mere matter of paper, yet it shifted real power toward the ordinary voter, who could now decide without an audience.

prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Locks required rare and costly materials that few towns could ever afford.
choices.rationale: The passage stresses humble means, not rare materials.

choices.text: Boats could always travel freely inland long before the lock was invented.
choices.rationale: The passage says elevation once blocked inland travel.

choices.text: Rivers were once the fastest possible way to move goods over long distances.
choices.rationale: The passage does not rank rivers as the fastest route.

choices.text: Canal locks let boats overcome changes in elevation, opening inland trade.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage explains how locks conquer elevation and thereby expand trade.

explanation: The lock's purpose and its effect on inland commerce are the passage's focus.

stimulus.title: Stairs for Boats
stimulus.text: Rivers do not run level, and for centuries that simple fact blocked boats from traveling far inland. The lock changed things. A lock is a chamber with gates at each end; a boat enters, the gates close, and water is let in or drained out until the boat rises or falls to the next stretch of river. String several locks together, and a vessel can climb a hillside the way a person climbs a staircase. The engineering is humble, relying on nothing more exotic than gravity and patience, yet it knit distant towns into trading partners and turned shallow rivers into highways of commerce.

prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: The market declined because several stalls closed at around the same time.
choices.rationale: The passage notes that not a single other stall had closed.

choices.text: Mr. Owusu's daughter took over the stall and ran it just as he had.
choices.rationale: The daughter notices his gift; the passage does not say she took over.

choices.text: Mr. Owusu succeeded mainly because his vegetables cost less than his rivals' did.
choices.rationale: The passage says it was not his prices that set him apart.

choices.text: Mr. Owusu's attentiveness to customers, not his produce, made his stall special.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage stresses that customers returned because he knew and remembered them.

explanation: The passage's point is that personal attentiveness, not produce, drew customers back.

stimulus.title: The Stall That Listened
stimulus.text: Every Saturday, Mr. Owusu set out the same vegetables on the same table, and for years his stall was just one among many. What set him apart, his daughter noticed, was not his prices but his memory. He recalled which customer's child disliked onions, who was cooking for a crowd that weekend, who had been ill and needed something gentle. He would set aside a perfect tomato for one regular and toss an extra handful of beans to another. People did not return only for the produce; they returned because, at his stall, they were known. When he finally retired, the market felt larger and lonelier, though not a single other stall had closed.

prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Black pepper has always been a cheap and easily available kitchen ingredient.
choices.rationale: The passage says spices were once nearly as valuable as silver.

choices.text: Sailors avoided long voyages because the spice trade was already too crowded.
choices.rationale: The high prices drove sailors to seek new routes, not avoid voyages.

choices.text: European merchants invented spices and were the first ever to harvest them.
choices.rationale: Merchants traded spices; they did not invent or first harvest them.

choices.text: The high cost of distant spices spurred voyages that eventually made spices common.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage links costly, rare spices to voyages that made them ordinary.

explanation: The passage traces spices from costly rarity to abundance through new sea routes.

stimulus.title: The Price of Pepper
stimulus.text: There was a time when a handful of black pepper could rival a handful of silver. The spice grew only in distant lands, and by the time it reached a European market it had passed through many hands, each adding a markup. Merchants guarded their routes jealously and spread tall tales about how spices were harvested, partly to discourage rivals. The high prices drove sailors to seek their own sea paths to the source, voyages that redrew the map of the world. In the end, the very abundance those voyages produced made spices ordinary, and the fortunes built on rarity quietly dissolved.

prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Lichens are the only living things able to survive on exposed rock surfaces.
choices.rationale: The passage does not claim lichens are the only rock survivors.

choices.text: Lichens prepare bare rock for later plants by helping form the first soil.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage shows lichens building the soil that lets later plants grow.

choices.text: Lichens compete with one another for the limited sunlight on a rock.
choices.rationale: Competition among lichens is not the focus.

choices.text: Mosses and small plants arrive on bare rock before any lichen does.
choices.rationale: The passage says lichens come first and mosses follow.

explanation: The passage frames the lichen as a pioneer that makes soil for what comes next.

stimulus.title: First on the Rock
stimulus.text: When a bare rock is left exposed, the first life to arrive is often a lichen, a strange partnership of fungus and alga living as one. The fungus grips the stone and gathers moisture; the alga, sheltered inside, makes food from sunlight. Together they need no soil at all. As a lichen grows, it slowly releases acids that crack the rock surface, and its dead tissue mixes with grit to form the first thin crumbs of soil. Years later, mosses and small plants can take root in that beginning. The lichen will likely be crowded out by the very community it made possible, an unsung founder of the green world that follows.

prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: The price of books dropped instantly once Gutenberg's printing press appeared.
choices.rationale: The passage explicitly says costs did not fall overnight.

choices.text: Scribes abandoned their work as soon as the first printing presses were built.
choices.rationale: It notes scholars still prized handwritten volumes, so scribes did not vanish at once.

choices.text: Gutenberg's reusable metal type made books far easier to reproduce and to spread.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage emphasizes how reusable type transformed the reproduction and reach of books.

choices.text: Handwritten books remained more beautiful and more highly valued than any printed book.
choices.rationale: Beauty of handwriting is not the passage's claim.

explanation: The passage frames the press as a turning point in how widely texts could circulate.

stimulus.title: Letters of Lead
stimulus.text: Before the 1450s, a book in Europe was copied by hand, a task that could occupy a scribe for a year. Johannes Gutenberg changed that arithmetic. By casting individual letters in metal, he could arrange them into a page, print hundreds of copies, then rearrange the same letters for the next page. The cost of a book did not fall overnight, and many scholars still prized handwritten volumes. But within fifty years, presses across the continent had produced millions of books. Ideas that once crept from city to city now traveled in bulk, and a reader in one town could hold the exact words read by a stranger far away.
